reason: The sources provide dozens of rich, cross-verified technical and historical details about humanity's 1974 interstellar transmission.
story: On November 16, 1974, astronomers gathered in Puerto Rico to celebrate upgrades to the giant Arecibo radio telescope by beaming humanity's first intentional interstellar radio message into deep space. Designed primarily by astronomer Frank Drake with assistance from Carl Sagan and Cornell researchers, the broadcast lasted under three minutes. It transmitted exactly 1,679 binary bits at 2,380 megahertz. Formatted into a grid of 73 by 23 characters, the decoded ones and zeros formed a graphic depicting numbers, DNA chemistry, the double helix, a human stick figure, the solar system with Earth offset, and the telescope itself. Drake aimed the signal at Messier 13, a globular star cluster 25,000 light-years away. However, the message was purely a symbolic tech demonstration: traveling at light speed, the signal will take 25,000 years to arrive, by which time the cluster will have shifted along its orbit.
angle: Humanity beamed an iconic cosmic postcard to a star cluster 25,000 light-years away, knowing the target will have moved out of the beam's center by the time the signal arrives.

claims.claim: The Arecibo message was transmitted into space on November 16, 1974.
The broadcast was sent from the Arecibo Observatory radio telescope in Puerto Rico.
The transmission was aimed at Messier 13 (M13), a globular star cluster located approximately 25,000 light-years from Earth.
The message was meant as a technological demonstration and symbolic event rather than a serious expectation of communicating with extraterrestrials.
The event marked a major ceremony celebrating remodeling and upgrades to the Arecibo telescope.
Astronomer Frank Drake was the primary designer and architect of the message.
Carl Sagan contributed to the design of the message.
Then-Cornell graduate student Richard Isaacman assisted Drake in crafting the transmission.
The entire message consisted of 1,679 binary digits.
The 1,679 bits were chosen because 1,679 is a semiprime number that arranges into a grid of 73 rows by 23 columns.
The message was broadcast at a radio frequency of 2,380 megahertz.
The binary digits were transmitted by frequency-shifting at a rate of 10 bits per second.
The entire transmission lasted less than three minutes.
The message encoded the numbers 1 to 10 in binary.
The transmission encoded the atomic numbers of hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and phosphorus, the elements composing DNA.
The message depicted a graphic of the double helix structure of DNA.
The message included an illustration of a human figure.
The graphic showed the Solar System with the third planet, Earth, offset to indicate where humanity lives.
The transmission concluded with a schematic graphic of the Arecibo radio telescope dish.
Because M13 orbits the galactic center, the cluster will have moved from its 1974 position by the time the transmission arrives.
Any round-trip reply from the target destination would take approximately 50,000 years.
In 2001, a crop circle hoax dubbed the 'Arecibo answer' appeared near the Chilbolton telescope in the UK, mimicking the message's grid with silicon and an alien head.

disputed: Whether the message will completely miss M13 or hit near its center: S5 and S6 state the cluster will have moved well out of the way, S2 notes most stars will have moved out of the beam, while S1 argues proper motion is small enough that the beam will still arrive near the center. Scripts should attribute this: 'while the cluster moves along its galactic orbit, astronomers disagree on whether the expanding beam will still clip its center.'

Whether Arecibo was the very first message sent into space: S2 and S3 note that earlier radar pulses and the 1962 Soviet Morse message bounced off Venus, but Arecibo was the first intentional transmission sent to an interstellar star cluster.
